beats.narration_text: Hi — this is Bella, for Chaitanya. This video is about how a student signs in once and can open every textbook they're entitled to. Every book is a separate site. None of them has your password.

show.event: cream Claude page; the serif greeting 'Hej, HAI' sets above the composer with the terracotta spark
the ask types itself into the composer, character by character
send button arms terracotta; runningText 'tracing the sign-in…' begins
three result lines land in order — the ask comes back ANSWERED, so the reel opens on a receipt, not a question
HAI H-mark bug settles lower-right at low opacity

props.command: Each of our textbooks is a separate website at its own address, and a student signs in once on the hub. Explain — for someone with no technical background — how a site that has never seen that student can know who they are and whether they are allowed in.
output: the hub writes a signed ticket — one book, one day
the textbook can't check the signature, so it calls home
logging out writes one timestamp that retires them all

beats.narration_text: Start with the shape of it. There's no one big website with all the textbooks inside. Each one is its own site, at its own address, on its own server. And a student should only sign in once.

show.event: a single large container outline draws — then dissolves, refusing the premise
four textbook site cards fan out from the centre, each with its own address bar, spaced apart with visible gaps between them
the sign-in box lands at the hub position in terracotta — the ONE accent
the gap between the sign-in box and the fanned sites is marked; no connectors exist yet

props.gapNote: no shared login, no shared server

beats.narration_text: So how does a separate website know who you are, and know you're allowed in? It has never seen you. It doesn't have your password. It has no idea who you are. It needs something it can be handed at the door. A ticket.

show.event: one textbook site card scales up to own the frame, a visitor silhouette waiting at its door
line one strikes through
line two strikes through
line three strikes through — all three now dead
the struck block fades back and the word 'ticket' types in terracotta serif beneath the door

denials: has no idea who you are

beats.narration_text: When a student clicks a textbook, the hub checks first: should this person be allowed in? If yes, it writes a ticket. Three things — who you are, which one book, and when it expires. Twenty-four hours.

show.event: two numbered slots appear at the hub

show.at: on 'should this person be allowed in'
show.event: slot one resolves to a tick — the access check passes BEFORE anything is written
slot two draws the ticket stub, perforated edge and all
stamp one lands: WHO
stamp two lands: WHICH BOOK — the word ONE is emphasised
stamp three lands in terracotta: EXPIRES · 24 HOURS, the accent of the beat

stamps.label: WHICH BOOK
stamps.value: one book, not all of them

beats.narration_text: And it's signed — not with a signature you could copy, but with a secret only the hub knows. Change one character and the signature stops matching. Then the ticket is handed to the textbook.

show.event: a seal presses down onto the stub and settles in terracotta

show.at: on 'a secret only the hub knows'
show.event: the seal's source is traced back to the hub, which alone holds it
one glyph of the stub's PLACEHOLDER identifier visibly flips
the seal cracks and greys; a persistent small caption reads 'example — not a real ticket'
an intact stub slides right, out of the hub and into the textbook site card

props.secretNote: a secret only the hub knows

beats.narration_text: Here's the surprising part. The textbook doesn't trust that ticket on its own. It can't — it doesn't know the secret, so it can't tell a real signature from a forged one. Holding a ticket and checking one are different powers.

show.event: the frame splits into two columns — HUB left, TEXTBOOK right
the hub column fills with both the ticket and the seal; the textbook column holds the ticket and an empty seal slot

show.at: on 'real signature from a forged one'
show.event: two stubs slide into the textbook column, identical on their face; the site cannot sort them and both stay unmarked
the two column headers resolve — HOLDS IT / CAN CHECK IT — with the empty slot in terracotta

beats.narration_text: So it asks the hub directly: is this ticket real, and is this person allowed in my book? The hub runs six checks in order and answers yes or no. Only then does the textbook let the student in, and remember them for later pages.

show.event: a dotted arc draws from the textbook back to the hub, carrying the ticket
six rows tick down one at a time, top to bottom, in the hub's own order
the arc reverses and a single green tick returns along it
the textbook's door opens
a small 'remembered for this visit' chip settles on the textbook so later pages skip the round trip

props.question: is this ticket real, and is this person allowed in my book?
checks: the student's account is still active
it was issued after their last logout
the book exists, and it's this book
this student is allowed in this book

beats.narration_text: Which leaves one hard problem. What happens when someone logs out? The tickets are already out there. Each one is valid for twenty-four hours, sitting on a site the hub doesn't control. You can't reach into a textbook site and snatch a ticket back. Logging out of the hub, by itself, changes nothing.

show.event: the fan of textbook sites returns, each now holding a stub with its own live countdown

show.at: on 'a site the hub doesn't control'
show.event: a boundary line draws around the hub; every stub sits OUTSIDE it
a reach from the hub extends toward a stub and stops at the boundary
the log-out press lands at the hub — and the countdowns keep running, unchanged

beats.narration_text: The obvious fix is a list of cancelled tickets, checked every time. That works. It also means keeping a list, keeping it in sync everywhere, keeping it fast, and keeping it forever. You've traded one hard problem for a permanent one. That is the moment to ask whether the list is necessary at all.

show.event: a list panel opens and starts filling with cancelled entries
a tick lands on the panel — the design is conceded, not strawmanned
copies of the list replicate out to every site
four cost labels stack: KEEP IT · EVERYWHERE · FAST · FOREVER, the last in terracotta
the list overruns the bottom of its panel and keeps growing off-frame

beats.narration_text: This system does something simpler. When you log out, it writes down one thing: the time you logged out. After that, any ticket issued before that moment is dead. Not cancelled — just older than your logout, so it no longer counts. One timestamp instead of a list. Every outstanding ticket, everywhere, invalid the instant you log out.

show.event: the sprawling list from the previous beat collapses into a SINGLE field in the student's record
one timestamp writes into that field in terracotta — the accent of the beat
a cutoff line sweeps across the row of outstanding tickets at the timestamp's position
every stub left of the line greys out simultaneously — not struck, not removed, simply no longer counting
the greyed field count resolves to 1 beside the dead list's growing count
a ticket issued AFTER the line stays live, proving the rule is the cutoff and not a purge

beats.narration_text: One Sign-In, Many Books. That's the mechanism, end to end. The full video adds the recap and a prompt you can run on your own service. The link is right below.
